claims.statement: Yatagarasu is a three-legged crow from Japanese myth.
claims.statement_id: Yatagarasu adalah gagak berkaki tiga dari mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: This is a statue of the Yatagarasu, a three-legged crow from Japanese myth.

claims.statement: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki portray it as Amaterasu’s servant.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki menampilkannya sebagai pelayan Amaterasu.
claims.quote: In the ancient Japanese chronicles Kojiki and Nihon shoki, the Yatagarasu appeared as a servant of Amaterasu-no-Okami, the goddess of the sun.

claims.statement: It was sent to guide Jimmu from Kumano to Nara.
claims.statement_id: Ia diutus membimbing Jimmu dari Kumano ke Nara.
claims.quote: It was sent to guide the legendary first emperor Jimmu from Kumano to present-day Nara

claims.statement: Kamigamo tradition says Kamo Taketsunumi took yatagarasu form to guide Jimmu.
claims.statement_id: Tradisi Kamigamo menyebut Kamo Taketsunumi menjelma sebagai yatagarasu untuk membimbing Jimmu.
claims.quote: Kamo Taketsunumi no Mikoto, a deity most renowned for taking the form of a three-legged crow (yatagarasu) and serving as a guide to Emperor Jinmu

claims.statement: Legend says it returned to Kumano Nachi Taisha.
claims.statement_id: Legenda menyebutnya kembali ke Kuil Kumano Nachi Taisha.
claims.quote: According to legend, the Yatagarasu then returned here, to the site of Kumano Nachi Taisha Grand Shrine.

claims.statement: The shrine’s Yatagarasu Stone is said to be its resting form.
claims.statement_id: Batu Yatagarasu di kuil dianggap sebagai wujudnya yang beristirahat.
claims.quote: contains the Yatagarasu-ishi (Yatagarasu Stone), said to be the resting form of the Yatagarasu.

claims.statement: Yatagarasu is called a guiding deity and servant of Kumano deities.
claims.statement_id: Yatagarasu disebut dewa penuntun dan pelayan dewa-dewa Kumano.
claims.quote: The Yatagarasu is both a deity of guidance and a servant of the Kumano deities, including Amaterasu-no-Okami.

claims.statement: The three-legged crow became an emblem of Kumano shrines.
claims.statement_id: Gagak berkaki tiga menjadi lambang kuil-kuil Kumano.
claims.quote: The three-legged crow has since become an emblem of Kumano shrines across Japan, representing rebirth and rejuvenation.

claims.statement: Yatagarasu appears in Japan’s national soccer team logos.
claims.statement_id: Yatagarasu digunakan pada logo tim sepak bola nasional Jepang.
claims.quote: The Yatagarasu is also used in the logo of Japan’s national men’s and women’s soccer teams.

claims.statement: A subsidiary shrine honors Yatagarasu’s resting place.
claims.statement_id: Kuil cabang didirikan untuk menghormati tempat peristirahatan Yatagarasu.
claims.quote: A subsidiary shrine called Miagatahiko-sha was erected on the grounds of Nachi Taisha to honor the resting place of the Yatagarasu.

issues.message: Diusulkan dilewati: Gashadokuro adalah ciptaan penulis majalah Saitō Morihiro pada 1966; kajian akademik tidak menemukan rekam tradisi historis sebelumnya. Item baru ini tidak memenuhi syarat sebagai makhluk dari mitologi, cerita rakyat, atau agama tradisional. (https://nirc.nanzan-u.ac.jp/journal/6/article/2314/pdf/download).

claims.statement: The Kojiki calls Hoderi the name of Umisachi, Konohana Sakuyahime’s first child.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menyebut Hoderi nama Umisachi dan putra pertama Konohana Sakuyahime.
claims.quote: Kojiki states that Umisachi's proper name was Hoderi no mikoto, the first of the three children produced by Konohana Sakuyahime.

claims.statement: Hoderi is a child of Ninigi and Konohana Sakuyahime.
claims.statement_id: Hoderi adalah putra Ninigi dan Konohana Sakuyahime.
claims.quote: An offspring of Ninigi and Konohana Sakuyahime.

claims.statement: Umisachi is Yamasachi’s elder brother.
claims.statement_id: Umisachi adalah kakak Yamasachi.
claims.quote: Umisachi ("sea-treasure") was the elder brother to Yamasachi ("mountain-treasure"; otherwise known as Hohodemi)

claims.statement: Many Nihon Shoki variants call Umisachi Hosuseri.
claims.statement_id: Banyak versi Nihon Shoki menyebut Umisachi sebagai Hosuseri.
claims.quote: Most of the variant accounts recorded by Nihongi, however, state that the kami Umisachi was Hosuseri-the second child born to Sakuyahime in the Kojiki account.

claims.statement: Yamasachi borrows Umisachi’s hook and loses it.
claims.statement_id: Yamasachi meminjam kail Umisachi dan menghilangkannya.
claims.quote: Yamasachi-hiko sets out to fish with his brother’s hook, while Umisachi-hiko tries his hand at hunting. But Yamasachi-hiko loses the hook he has borrowed

claims.statement: Umisachi refuses replacement hooks.
claims.statement_id: Umisachi menolak kail pengganti.
claims.quote: He breaks up his sword and makes many new hooks, but Umisachi-hiko refuses to accept them.

claims.statement: Umisachi pledged to become Hohodemi’s protector and vassal.
claims.statement_id: Umisachi berjanji menjadi pelindung dan pengikut Hohodemi.
claims.quote: he pledged to become Hohodemi's protector and vassal.

claims.statement: Yamasachi uses tide jewels to make Umisachi yield.
claims.statement_id: Yamasachi memakai permata pengatur pasang untuk membuat Umisachi menyerah.
claims.quote: Yamasachi-hiko uses the orbs given to him by the god of the sea and calls in the tide, almost drowning Umisachi-hiko, who finally relents.

claims.statement: Ushiodake Shrine enshrines Umisachi-hiko.
claims.statement_id: Kuil Ushiodake memuja Umisachi-hiko.
claims.quote: Ushiodake Shrine is the only Shinto sanctuary in Japan that enshrines Umisachi-hiko

claims.statement: Shrine dances retell the Umisachi-Yamasachi myth.
claims.statement_id: Tarian kagura di kuil itu menceritakan kembali mitos Umisachi dan Yamasachi.
claims.quote: The dances include a retelling of the Umisachi-Yamasachi myth and other ancient legends

claims.statement: Umisachi’s mother set fire to her birthing hut and he was born at the height of the flames.
claims.statement_id: Ibu Umisachi membakar pondok bersalin dan ia lahir ketika api memuncak.
claims.quote: Umisachi's mother set fire to her parturition hut, whereupon Umisachi was born as the flames reached their peak.

claims.statement: Jorōgumo is a yōkai that can appear as a woman.
claims.statement_id: Jorōgumo adalah yōkai yang dapat berubah menjadi perempuan.
claims.quote: Jorōgumo (Japanese: 絡新婦 (kanji), じょろうぐも (hiragana)) is a type of yōkai, a creature of Japanese folklore. It can shapeshift into a beautiful woman

claims.statement: Edo-period tales depict jorōgumo changing into women.
claims.statement_id: Kisah zaman Edo menggambarkan jorōgumo berubah menjadi perempuan.
claims.quote: In Edo period writings such as the Taihei-Hyakumonogatari (太平百物語) and the Tonoigusa (宿直草), there are "jorogumo" that shapeshift into women.

claims.statement: In one story a warrior strikes her and she flees to an attic.
claims.statement_id: Dalam satu kisah, prajurit memukul sosok itu dan ia lari ke loteng.
claims.quote: The warrior sees through her ploy and, realizing she is a yōkai, strikes her with his sword, making her flee to the attic.

claims.statement: A large spider is found dead in the attic.
claims.statement_id: Laba-laba besar ditemukan mati di loteng.
claims.quote: The next day, they find a dead jorōgumo one or two shaku long in the attic, along with numerous bodies of people that the jorōgumo had devoured.

claims.statement: Magoroku finds a small spider and web afterward.
claims.statement_id: Magoroku mendapati laba-laba kecil dan jaring setelah peristiwa itu.
claims.quote: Concluding it was only a dream, Magoroku looked around and noticed a small joro spider that had made a tight web around the eaves.

claims.statement: Sekien’s illustrated book was first published in 1776.
claims.statement_id: Buku ilustrasi Sekien terbit pada 1776.
claims.quote: Published in 1776, Gazu hyakki yagyō was followed by Konjaku gazu zoku hyakki in 1777

claims.statement: Sekien’s illustration shows a spider-legged woman surrounded by smaller spiders.
claims.statement_id: Ilustrasi Sekien menampilkan perempuan berkaki laba-laba dikelilingi laba-laba kecil.
claims.quote: Toriyama Sekien’s “Jorōgumo” overlays spider legs onto the robed body of a woman with long hair, surrounded by a swarm of tiny spiders.

claims.statement: The illustration has no written description of supernatural abilities.
claims.statement_id: Ilustrasi itu tidak disertai uraian tentang kekuatan gaib.
claims.quote: Sekien provided no accompanying text outlining supernatural abilities.

claims.statement: Jorōgumo is also a name used for real spiders.
claims.statement_id: Jorōgumo juga menjadi nama bagi laba-laba sungguhan.
claims.quote: Jorōgumo can also refer to some species of spiders, such as the Nephila and Argiope spiders.

claims.statement: Waterside spider tales are distinct from Edo ghost stories.
claims.statement_id: Cerita laba-laba di perairan berbeda dari kisah hantu zaman Edo.
claims.quote: Waterside legends of spiders casting silk threads are similarly distinct from early modern ghost tales rather than subsequent episodes of a shared life story.

claims.statement: In Tonoigusa it appears as a young woman with an infant.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Tonoigusa jorōgumo menyamar sebagai perempuan muda yang membawa bayi.
claims.quote: In Tonoigusa, the jorōgumo appears at a house at night in the guise of a young woman holding an infant.

claims.statement: In Magoroku’s tale a girl asks him to marry despite his marriage.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah Magoroku, seorang gadis memintanya menikah meski ia sudah menikah.
claims.quote: a 16- or 17-year-old girl asked him to marry her. Already married, he declined, but the girl persisted.

claims.statement: Kagutsuchi is the fire god linked to Izanami’s death.
claims.statement_id: Kagutsuchi adalah dewa api yang terkait dengan kematian Izanami.
claims.quote: After burying Izanami, Izanagi turns toward Kagutsuchi, the fire god who caused the tragedy.

claims.statement: Izanami died after giving birth to the fire god and entered Yomi.
claims.statement_id: Izanami meninggal seusai melahirkan dewa api lalu masuk ke Yomi.
claims.quote: When the goddess died after giving birth to the god of fire, she entered the world of darkness called Yomi-no-kuni.

claims.statement: Izanagi beheaded Kagutsuchi with his sword.
claims.statement_id: Izanagi memenggal Kagutsuchi dengan pedangnya.
claims.quote: Filled with wrath, he pulls his sword and beheads Kagutsuchi with a single swing.

claims.statement: Blood from the sword and Kagutsuchi’s body each gave rise to eight deities.
claims.statement_id: Darah pedang dan tubuh Kagutsuchi masing-masing melahirkan delapan dewa.
claims.quote: Blood drips from the blade onto the ground, producing eight new deities, while eight others emerge from Kagutsuchi’s maimed body.

claims.statement: The emergent deities are linked to rocks, swords, thunder, flames, waterfalls, and valleys.
claims.statement_id: Dewa-dewa yang lahir berkaitan dengan batu, pedang, petir, api, air terjun, dan lembah.
claims.quote: These are the gods of rocks, swords, thunder, flames, waterfalls, and valleys

claims.statement: Akiha Gongendō enshrines Hi no Kagutsuchi no Kami, associated with fire prevention.
claims.statement_id: Akiha Gongendō memuja Hi no Kagutsuchi no Kami, terkait pencegahan kebakaran.
claims.quote: The enshrined kami (Shinto deity) is Hi no Kagutsuchi no Kami, who is associated with fire prevention and appears in one of the earliest written records of Japan.

claims.statement: Residents gather twice a year to pray for protection from fire and calamities.
claims.statement_id: Warga berkumpul dua kali setahun untuk memohon perlindungan dari api dan bencana.
claims.quote: Local residents gather there twice a year to pray for protection from fire and other calamities.

claims.statement: He is called Akiha Daigongen in Buddhism and Akiha-san locally.
claims.statement_id: Nama Buddhisnya Akiha Daigongen dan sebutan setempat Akiha-san.
claims.quote: Hi no Kagutsuchi no Kami is also known by the Buddhist name “Akiha Daigongen,” and he is known locally as “Akiha-san.”

claims.statement: Akiba Shrine in Ogimachi was dedicated to Kagutsuchi in the Taishō era.
claims.statement_id: Kuil Akiba di Ogimachi didedikasikan kepada Kagutsuchi pada zaman Taishō.
claims.quote: This sanctuary remained a modest place of worship until the Taisho era (1912–1926), when the shrine building was reconstructed and officially dedicated to Kagutsuchi, the Shinto god of fire.

claims.statement: Some identified Mt. Daisen’s great deity as Kagutsuchi.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian orang mengenali dewa Gunung Daisen sebagai Kagutsuchi.
claims.quote: The God was believed by many to be the Kagutsuchi-no-mikoto, or God of Fire.

claims.statement: Kamaitachi is a yōkai and can also refer to the strange event itself.
claims.statement_id: Kamaitachi adalah yōkai yang juga dapat menyebut kejadian aneh penyebab luka.
claims.quote: is a Japanese yōkai from the oral tradition of the Kōshin'etsu region. It can also refer to the strange events that this creature causes.

claims.statement: Kamaitachi is associated with whirlwinds and skin cuts.
claims.statement_id: Kamaitachi dikaitkan dengan pusaran angin dan sayatan kulit.
claims.quote: Kama-itachi are yokai said to ride dust devils or sudden whirlwinds, slicing human skin as if by a blade.

claims.statement: The wounds may at first be painless or bloodless.
claims.statement_id: Lukanya dapat awalnya tidak sakit atau berdarah.
claims.quote: Victims often feel little pain at first and may not bleed until later.

claims.statement: The name combines the words for sickle and weasel.
claims.statement_id: Namanya diterangkan sebagai gabungan kata sabit dan cerpelai.
claims.quote: The name is a combination of the words kama (sickle), and itachi (weasel).

claims.statement: Edo-era pictures show sickle-clawed weasels, but local explanations differ.
claims.statement_id: Gambar sejak zaman Edo menunjukkan cerpelai bercakar seperti sabit, tetapi tafsir daerah beragam.
claims.quote: From the Edo period on, they’re depicted as weasels with sickle-like claws, though explanations vary by region—some attribute the cuts to the phenomenon itself, to wind deities, or to minor spirits.

claims.statement: Hida tales have three deities trip, cut, and treat a victim.
claims.statement_id: Cerita Hida menghadirkan tiga dewa yang menjatuhkan, menyayat, lalu mengoleskan obat.
claims.quote: In Hida, three deities travel together: the first trips the victim, the second slashes, and the third applies a salve, so there’s no immediate pain or bleeding.

claims.statement: Shin’etsu links the injury to an evil deity and a calendar taboo.
claims.statement_id: Di Shin’etsu luka dikaitkan dengan dewa jahat dan pantangan menginjak kalender.
claims.quote: In Shin’etsu, the injuries are blamed on a malevolent deity, and stepping on a calendar was warned to invite misfortune.

claims.statement: In Tōhoku charred calendar paper was a folk remedy.
claims.statement_id: Di Tōhoku abu kalender tua dipercaya dapat mengobati luka.
claims.quote: In Tohoku, applying the charred remains of an old calendar to the wound was said to cure it.

claims.statement: Related terms include nogama in Kōchi and kama-kaze elsewhere.
claims.statement_id: Istilah terkait meliputi nogama di Kōchi dan kama-kaze di daerah lain.
claims.quote: Related terms and interpretations include “nogama” in Kochi and “kama-kaze” in other regions.

claims.statement: Hida’s three figures are described as deities rather than weasels.
claims.statement_id: Kisah tiga dewa di Hida dibedakan dari gambaran cerpelai.
claims.quote: In Hida, in the Niu River basin, they are said in legends to be a company of three evil gods.

claims.statement: A popular depiction has the small yōkai ride wind and cut skin.
claims.statement_id: Gambaran populer menyebut yōkai kecil ini menunggang angin dan menyayat kulit.
claims.quote: This small, mammal-like yōkai rides on the wind, slicing at the flesh of mortals with its bladed limbs.

claims.statement: She is Ōyamatsumi’s daughter and Ninigi’s wife.
claims.statement_id: Ia putri Ōyamatsumi dan istri Ninigi.
claims.quote: The daughter of Ōyamatsumi (according to the main text of Nihongi, the offspring of Ōyamatsumi and a heavenly kami). Married to Ninigi

claims.statement: Her tree-flower name is associated with cherry blossoms.
claims.statement_id: Namanya berarti bunga pohon dan dikaitkan dengan bunga sakura.
claims.quote: The name Konohana ("tree-flower") refers to the short-lived beauty of the cherry blossom

claims.statement: She is contrasted with her long-lived elder sister Iwanagahime.
claims.statement_id: Ia dibandingkan dengan kakaknya Iwanagahime yang berumur panjang.
claims.quote: was given in contrast to Konohana's older sister Iwanagahime, who was ugly but long-lived.

claims.statement: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki place their meeting at Cape Kasasa.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki menempatkan pertemuan mereka di Tanjung Kasasa.
claims.quote: According to both Kojiki and Nihongi, Ninigi met the beautiful maiden Sakuyahime at Cape Kasasa

claims.statement: Ninigi doubted her pregnancy after one night.
claims.statement_id: Ninigi meragukan kehamilan setelah satu malam.
claims.quote: Ninigi, however, was surprised at her claim to have become pregnant in a single night, and suspected that the child was actually the offspring of an earthly kami

claims.statement: She set fire to her birthing hut to prove the child’s heavenly descent.
claims.statement_id: Ia membakar pondok bersalin untuk membuktikan keturunan dewa langit.
claims.quote: Shamed and enraged at Ninigi's accusation, Sakuyahime entered a doorless parturition hut, setting fire to it with the vow that the child should not be injured if it were truly the offspring of the heavenly kami Ninigi.

claims.statement: The Kojiki names her three children Hoderi, Hosuseri, and Hoori.
claims.statement_id: Dalam versi Kojiki ia melahirkan Hoderi, Hosuseri, dan Hoori.
claims.quote: Inside the hut, Sakuyahime gave birth to three kami, including Hoderi, Hosuseri, and Hoori (according to Kojiki; the names differ somewhat in the various other accounts).

claims.statement: She is enshrined at Fuji’s Asama Shrine.
claims.statement_id: Ia dipuja di Kuil Asama di Fuji.
claims.quote: Konohana Sakuyahime is one of the enshrined deities (saijin) at Fuji's Asama Jinja.

claims.statement: Her identification with Mt. Fuji’s deity dates to the early seventeenth century.
claims.statement_id: Penyamaan dengan dewa Fuji berasal dari awal abad ke-17.
claims.quote: The identification of the deity of Mt. Fuji with the Shinto deity Konohanasakuya Hime dates from the early seventeenth century.

claims.statement: A 1788 amulet showed Amida, while an 1860 one showed a Shinto goddess.
claims.statement_id: Jimat 1788 menampilkan Amida, sedangkan jimat 1860 menampilkan dewi Shinto.
claims.quote: The go-o dated 1788 depicts Amida Nyorai with attendants above Mt. Fuji. In the go-o dated 1860, Amida Nyorai has been replaced by a female Shinto deity.

claims.statement: Older statues were interpreted as her images by the nineteenth century.
claims.statement_id: Pada abad ke-19 patung lama pun ditafsirkan sebagai sosoknya.
claims.quote: By the nineteenth century, even older statues like the one enshrined at Shibokusa Sengen-jinja Shrine were viewed as depictions of Konohanasakuya Hime.

claims.statement: Fuji and Asama or Sengen shrines came to identify their deity with her almost universally.
claims.statement_id: Penyamaan dewa Fuji dan dewa kuil Sengen atau Asama dengannya menjadi hampir universal.
claims.quote: Soon, the deity of Mt. Fuji—and the deity worshiped at Sengen or Asama shrines across the country—came to be identified almost universally with Konohanasakuya Hime.

claims.statement: The Shinto-Buddhist separation policy came in 1868 after the shift at Fuji.
claims.statement_id: Kebijakan pemisahan Shinto dan Buddha terjadi pada 1868 setelah perubahan penekanan di Fuji.
claims.quote: At Mt. Fuji, this shift in emphasis to a female Shinto deity came long before the government-ordered separation of Buddhism and Shinto in 1868.

claims.statement: Noppera-bō is a humanlike faceless yōkai.
claims.statement_id: Noppera-bō adalah yōkai yang tampak manusia tetapi tanpa wajah.
claims.quote: in Japanese folklore, is a faceless yōkai that looks like a human but has no face.

claims.statement: It first looks ordinary, then shows a smooth blank face.
claims.statement_id: Mula-mula ia tampak biasa, lalu wajahnya menjadi licin tanpa ciri.
claims.quote: They appear at first as ordinary human beings, sometimes impersonating someone familiar to the victim, before causing their features to disappear, leaving a blank, smooth sheet of skin where their face should be.

claims.statement: Hearn’s woman has no eyes, nose, or mouth.
claims.statement_id: Sosok perempuan dalam cerita Hearn tidak punya mata, hidung, atau mulut.
claims.quote: she had no eyes or nose or mouth,--and he screamed and ran away.

claims.statement: Noppera-bō chiefly frightens people.
claims.statement_id: Noppera-bō terutama menakut-nakuti manusia.
claims.quote: Noppera-bō are known primarily for frightening humans, but are usually otherwise harmless.

claims.statement: Some tales attribute the apparition to a disguised mujina, fox, or tanuki.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian cerita mengaitkan penampakan itu dengan samaran mujina, rubah, atau tanuki.
claims.quote: Often, a noppera-bō would not actually exist, but was the disguise of a mujina, a fox kitsune, or a tanuki

claims.statement: Hearn’s “Mujina” appeared in Kwaidan in 1904.
claims.statement_id: Kisah terkenal “Mujina” karya Hearn terbit dalam Kwaidan pada 1904.
claims.quote: An iconic story about a noppera-bō (though this name does not appear in the story) is "Mujina" in Lafcadio Hearn's book Kwaidan (1904).

claims.statement: The merchant sees a woman crying beside the moat.
claims.statement_id: Pedagang melihat perempuan menangis di tepi parit.
claims.quote: he perceived a woman crouching by the moat, all alone, and weeping bitterly.

claims.statement: The woman turns and strokes her face.
claims.statement_id: Perempuan itu berbalik lalu mengusap wajah.
claims.quote: Then that O-jochu turned around, and dropped her sleeve, and stroked her face with her hand

claims.statement: The merchant then reaches a soba seller.
claims.statement_id: Pedagang kemudian mendekati penjual soba.
claims.quote: It proved to be only the lantern of an itinerant soba-seller

claims.statement: The soba seller’s face becomes egg-like and the light goes out.
claims.statement_id: Penjual soba juga mengusap wajah hingga licin seperti telur dan cahaya padam.
claims.quote: cried the soba-man, stroking his own face--which therewith became like unto an Egg... And, simultaneously, the light went out.

claims.statement: Hearn’s main story text calls the faceless figure mujina rather than noppera-bō.
claims.statement_id: Teks utama Hearn memakai istilah mujina, bukan noppera-bō.
claims.quote: In Lafcadio Hearn's story, the faceless being is not called a noppera-bō but a mujina

claims.statement: A 1767 collection records a nupperibō apparition.
claims.statement_id: Kumpulan kisah tahun 1767 mencatat penampakan bernama nupperibō.
claims.quote: One tale that hints at some shapeshifting magic beast tricking humans into seeing faceless beings occurs in kaidan collection Shinsetsu Hyakumonogatari (Meiwa 4/1767). It records that the nupperibō (ぬっぺりほう) made spooky appearance in Nijōgawara, Kyoto

claims.statement: Hearn’s own note calls the apparition “nopperabo.”
claims.statement_id: Catatan Hearn menyebut penampakan itu “nopperabo”.
claims.quote: An apparition with a smooth, totally featureless face, called a "nopperabo," is a stock part of the Japanese pantheon of ghosts and demons.

claims.statement: Hearn sets the tale at Kii-no-kuni-zaka.
claims.statement_id: Kisah Hearn berlatar di lereng Kii-no-kuni-zaka.
claims.quote: On the Akasaka Road, in Tokyo, there is a slope called Kii-no-kuni-zaka

claims.statement: Takemikazuchi arose from blood on Izanagi’s sword after Kagutsuchi was killed.
claims.statement_id: Takemikazuchi lahir dari darah pada pedang Izanagi setelah Kagutsuchi dibunuh.
claims.quote: A kami produced from the blood adhering to the sword when Izanagi killed the fire kami Kagutsuchi.

claims.statement: He asked Ōkuninushi to yield Izumo to the heavenly kami.
claims.statement_id: Ia meminta Ōkuninushi menyerahkan Izumo kepada dewa langit.
claims.quote: Takemikazuchi descended to the land of Izumo and entreated Ōkuninushi to transfer the land (kuniyuzuri) to the heavenly kami.

claims.statement: The Kojiki names Amanotorifune and Nihon Shoki names Futsunushi as his companion.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menyebut Amanotorifune dan Nihon Shoki menyebut Futsunushi sebagai pendamping.
claims.quote: Together with Amanotorifune (Kojiki) or Futsunushi no kami (Nihongi)

claims.statement: He defeated Takeminakata and drove him to Suwa.
claims.statement_id: Ia mengalahkan Takeminakata dan mendorongnya ke Suwa.
claims.quote: Kojiki adds that he engaged in a test of strength with Takeminakata, the child of Ōkuninushi, who had opposed the heavenly forces. Subduing Takeminaka, he drove him away to Suwa in the province of Shinano

claims.statement: He sent Futsunomitama to aid Jimmu.
claims.statement_id: Ia mengirim pedang Futsunomitama untuk menolong Jimmu.
claims.quote: On the occasion of Emperor Jinmu's eastern campaign, Takemikazuchi deferred from descending to aid Jinmu, but in his place sent his sword Futsunomitama

claims.statement: He is worshiped at Kashima and Kasuga.
claims.statement_id: Ia dipuja di Kashima dan Kasuga.
claims.quote: Takemikazuchi is worshiped at Kashima, Kasuga and other shrines.

claims.statement: The shrine tradition calls him a thunder god arriving from Kashima on a white deer to protect the capital.
claims.statement_id: Tradisi menyebutnya dewa petir yang datang dari Kashima dengan rusa putih untuk melindungi ibu kota.
claims.quote: According to legend, Takemikazuchi no Mikoto, the god of thunder, came to Nara during the early Nara period (710–784). In response to prayers for protection of the capital, he traveled from Kashima Jingu Shrine in Ibaraki Prefecture, close to present-day Tokyo, riding a white deer.

claims.statement: He and three other deities were enshrined when Kasuga was built in 768.
claims.statement_id: Ia bersama tiga dewa lain dipuja di Kasuga sejak pembangunan kuil pada 768.
claims.quote: These kami were enshrined here when a shrine was built on this hillside in 768.

claims.statement: Tamamo-no-Mae is a disguised fox favored at Retired Emperor Toba’s court.
claims.statement_id: Tamamo-no-Mae adalah samaran rubah istana yang disukai mantan Kaisar Toba.
claims.quote: a wicked golden fox with nine tails took the guise of an elegant court lady. Calling herself Tamamo no Mae, she served in the court of Retired Emperor Toba (1103–1156) and soon gained his favor.

claims.statement: A diviner unmasks the fox during Toba’s illness and it flees to Nasu.
claims.statement_id: Ahli ramal membongkar identitasnya saat Toba sakit, lalu ia lari ke Nasu.
claims.quote: When the Retired Emperor took ill, however, the fox’s identity was revealed by a court diviner, and it escaped to Nasu.

claims.statement: Imperial troops killed the fox after a battle.
claims.statement_id: Pasukan kaisar membunuh rubah itu setelah pertempuran.
claims.quote: After a long battle, the emperor’s troops killed the fox.

claims.statement: Legend says the fox’s body became the Killing Stone.
claims.statement_id: Dalam legenda tubuh rubah menjadi batu yang disebut Batu Pembunuh.
claims.quote: Its body transformed into a boulder, but the fox’s malevolence lived on: the boulder continued to exude an evil aura and noxious gases. Anything that lingered near the rock died, and it was thus dubbed the “Killing Stone.”

claims.statement: The stone lies near volcanic vents emitting toxic gases.
claims.statement_id: Batu berada dekat celah vulkanik dengan gas beracun.
claims.quote: The boulder sits beside one of Mt. Chausu’s volcanic vents, which emit sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide gases.

claims.statement: Early tellings portray Tamamo as a two-tailed fox.
claims.statement_id: Penuturan awal menyebut Tamamo rubah berekor dua.
claims.quote: In early tellings, she was a two-tailed fox.

claims.statement: The nine-tailed depiction dates to the Edo period.
claims.statement_id: Gambaran sembilan ekor muncul pada zaman Edo.
claims.quote: the concept that she was a nine-tailed fox in particular is of surprisingly recent origin, dating only back to the Edo period (1603–1868).

claims.statement: The Daji story merged with Tamamo’s legend in the Edo period.
claims.statement_id: Kisah Daji dari Tiongkok berpadu dengan kisah Tamamo pada pertengahan zaman Edo.
claims.quote: This story entered Japan in translation in the mid-Edo era, entwining itself with existing stories of Tamamo no Mae to transform her from a two- into a nine-tailed fox in the popular imagination.

claims.statement: The Smithsonian scroll shows her taking woman and nine-tailed fox forms.
claims.statement_id: Gulungan Smithsonian menampilkan perubahan antara perempuan dan rubah berekor sembilan.
claims.quote: She is capable of transforming herself into the guise of a beautiful woman, or into the form of a magical nine-tailed fox.

claims.statement: Nasu legend says Gennō broke the stone to weaken the spirit.
claims.statement_id: Legenda Nasu menceritakan Gennō memecahkan batu untuk melemahkan roh rubah.
claims.quote: Centuries later, the Buddhist monk Gennō (1329–1400) came to Nasu. Hoping to break the spirit’s power, he struck the stone with a great hammer, shattering it into three pieces.

claims.statement: The annual Gojinkasai rite appeases the fox spirit.
claims.statement_id: Upacara Gojinkasai tahunan masih dilakukan untuk menenangkan roh rubah.
claims.quote: Since then, a nighttime ritual called Gojinkasai has been conducted on the last Sunday in May to appease the fox’s spirit.

claims.statement: The Nasu boulder is called Sesshō-seki or Killing Stone.
claims.statement_id: Batu di Nasu bernama Sesshō-seki atau Batu Pembunuh.
claims.quote: This is the Sesshō-seki, or “Killing Stone”—a foreboding site steeped in local legend.

claims.statement: The nine-tailed Daji story comes from Chinese lore.
claims.statement_id: Kisah Daji berekor sembilan berasal dari tradisi Tiongkok.
claims.quote: In Chinese lore, Daji, favorite consort of King Zhou of Shang (r. 1075–1046 BCE), was a nine-tailed fox hellbent on destroying his reign.
